6c894a18-a494-45da-b7f6-c40073885d9c.title: A reasonably healthy diet can still put your gut at risk. A dietitian explains why
6c894a18-a494-45da-b7f6-c40073885d9c.incipit: Joshua Hinton is an actor and musician. The 27-year-old shares his day on a plate. Photo: Art by Eliza Iredale8.25am Start the day with a glass of water and two brown rice cakes...
6c894a18-a494-45da-b7f6-c40073885d9c.body: Joshua Hinton is an actor and musician. The 27-year-old shares his day on a plate. Photo: Art by Eliza Iredale 8.25am Start the day with a glass of water and two brown rice cakes topped with ham and cheese. After breakfast, I feed the dog and get ready for the day. 10.20am Another glass of water and a small bowl of assorted nuts. 12.35pm A ham and cheese toastie and a Coke Zero, while I prepare for some drama classes that I will be teaching that afternoon. 7.50pm A grilled chicken burrito and some fries on my way home from work. 9.10pm A glass of water and a few squares of dark chocolate while I watch TV. Dr Joanna McMillan says: Top marks for... Terrific snack choices – the nuts provide fibre, healthy fats and vitamin E, while the dark chocolate adds polyphenols and both are high in magnesium. A chicken burrito can also be a great takeaway choice if it comes loaded with salad, salsa and black beans. If you keep eating like this you’ll... Put your long-term gut health at risk. Processed meats, including ham, are best eaten as an occasional treat given their association with bowel cancer and the way they push up sodium levels. Combined with no fruit and few vegetables, you’re also missing the gut protection fibre and diverse plant compounds provide. Why don’t you try... Cutting back on the ham and filling your toastie with tuna, leftover roast chicken or other lean meat and sliced hard-boiled egg, then adding tomato, spinach or roasted veg. With the burrito, choose extra beans, salsa and salad and skip the fries most days. A healthier at-home alternative is skin-on potato wedges tossed in extra virgin olive oil and air-fried, which gives you more fibre and potassium without losing crispy-potato pleasure. Joshua Hinton’s A Place in the Sultan’s Kitchen plays at the Sydney Opera House, October 14-17. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning. Sign up for our newsletter. Nicole Economos is a Social Media Producer/Journalist for The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age. Connect via email . From our partners

0b4a9a0d-0ac1-4329-9b05-3628f3e4cc2a.title: Is it healthy to eat avocado every day? Dietitians explain
0b4a9a0d-0ac1-4329-9b05-3628f3e4cc2a.incipit: If you love starting the day with a plate of avocado toast, you might be wondering if it’s healthy to eat an...
0b4a9a0d-0ac1-4329-9b05-3628f3e4cc2a.body: Is it safe to eat avocado every day? How to eat avocado? If you love starting the day with a plate of avocado toast , you might be wondering if it’s healthy to eat an avocado a day. Many people know that these fruits are high in fat, but there’s more to the story. Ahead, dietitians explain the health benefits of avocado . Researchers have found that eating avocado can actually lower your risk of certain diseases, particularly if you’re using this fruit in place of a less nutritious ingredient, like butter. Additionally, avocados are surprisingly high in fibre. The NHS advises adults should aim for 30g of fibre a day; a single avocado comes in at 14 grams – nearly half of your daily recommended amount. Avocados are also high in certain vitamins and minerals your body needs to function optimally. That said, dietitians also note that there are some people who may need to be more thoughtful about avocado consumption. Ahead, dietitians explain what to know about avocados, including the nutrition facts, how many you can safely eat in a day, and ideas for how to use them. Avocado nutrition Gerri French , a nutritionist in Santa Barbara, California describes avocados as a 'wholesome food with lots of merit,' this popular fruit is grown in warm climates like Florida, Mexico and California, and is usually in season late spring through late summer. Despite having over 500 different types of avocado, the Hass variety is likely what you’ll find in the grocery store. Here's what you'll get on average in one peeled avocado: Calories: 322 Fat: 29g Fibre: 14g Carbohydrates: 17g Protein: 4g Is it safe to eat avocado every day? Yes, the numbers above make it look like avocados contain a lot of fat. However, they are rich in monounsaturated fats, which are considered healthy — especially for your heart. In fact, researchers from Harvard’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health found those who ate the equivalent of one avocado per week had a 16% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and a 21% lower risk of coronary heart disease compared to those who didn't eat any. They also discovered that people who replaced half a serving of margarine, butter, egg, yogurt, cheese or processed meats with the same amount of avocado every day had a 16 to 22% lower risk of heart disease. What's more, avocados have a low glycemic index if you’re monitoring your blood sugar. Interestingly, a 2023 study found those who had eaten avocado 2 days prior to the beginning of the study had a 20% lower risk of developing diabetes over 6 years than people who didn't eat avocado . People who were diagnosed with prediabetes and ate the avocado before the study had a 31% lower risk of developing full-blown diabetes in the 6-year follow-up. Danielle Daly Avocados are also packed with other nutrients such as folate, vitamin B6, vitamin C, vitamin K, manganese, copper, zinc, sodium, potassium, phosphorus, magnesium, iron and calcium. Avocados contain carotenoids such as beta-carotene (an antioxidant known to protect against some cancers and heart disease) as well as lutein and zeaxanthin (which are important for eye health, and preventing eye disease such as macular-degeneration). Overall, French says 'it’s okay for just about everyone to eat avocado every day, just not three avocados a day.' She recommends replacing a processed food you eat regularly with avocado. That said, there are certain conditions when individuals should not eat them every day. ' Anyone with kidney issues might need to watch the potassium and people on lower-fat or lower-calorie diets should keep portions in check,' says Brooke Loewenstein , a nutrition expert in New York City. In those cases, it's smart to be extra mindful of how much avocado you're eating. How to eat avocado First, make sure it's ripe: Give it a squeeze and a little give, with a dark green skin, means it's good to eat. If it’s hard as a rock, simply put the avocado in a paper bag, and place it on your window sill or your counter for a few days, and it’ll ripen right up . The next step is to cut it up , which requires a bit of finesse. Begin by slicing the avocado in half, lengthwise and carefully take out the pit. Then, use a spoon and scoop out the flesh of the avocado, and place on a cutting board. Finally, slice up the avocado into your desired thickness. In salads: Drizzle lemon juice on a fresh slice, sprinkle it with salt and pepper and then toss into your salad. In salsa: French enjoys eating avocados chopped up and mixed with beans, corn and tomatoes. On toast: Mash up your avo and then add seasonings like lemon pepper, garlic salt or cajun seasoning and spread it on your favorite bread. In smoothies: Blend avocado with leafy greens, a little fruit juice and water for a flavourful on-the-go smoothie. Grilled: Put slices on the grill and then top off your chicken. Baked: Bake avocados stuffed with a ground meat and cheese combo. French offers this caution though that while avocado is a nutritional choice, 'the company that it keeps can be the problem.' In other words, think about what you’re pairing it with. For example, adding avos to your fave salad, but then drowning it with processed salad dressing is not so healthy. Guacamole is another example. While guacamole is healthy, overeating chips with it every day is not. The bottom line The takeaway from the experts and from research is pretty clear: Avocados are fine to eat every day, with a caveat. 'Just because something’s healthy doesn’t mean more is better. Sticking to around 1⁄3 to 1⁄2 an avocado keeps things balanced without going overboard on calories or fat,' says Loewenstein. So whether you slice it, dice it, blend it, mash it, grill it, bake it or fry it, avocado can be a healthy addition to most eating plans. Laura Iu, R.D., is a registered dietitian nutritionist, certified intuitive eating counselor, yoga guide, and owner of Laura Iu Nutrition, a private practice in New York City. She earned her Bachelor of Science in Nutrition and Dietetics from New York University and completed her internship in dietetics at Weill Cornell & Columbia Medical Center of New York-Presbyterian Hospital. She went on to work in New York City’s top hospitals, including Mount Sinai Hospital and NYU Langone Health. She believes that true health is all encompassing — physical, emotional, and mental wellbeing — not an external measure via shape or size.

50b361f3-cbda-4c26-8536-a761eeb8dd74.title: 'I've been taking expensive probiotics every day' — the supplement may not be doing what you think
50b361f3-cbda-4c26-8536-a761eeb8dd74.incipit: Medical School found that for healthy people, eating fiber-rich foods such as whole grains, vegetables and fruit is more beneficial than probiotic...
50b361f3-cbda-4c26-8536-a761eeb8dd74.body: Research published Thursday by the University of Michigan - Medical School found that for healthy people, eating fiber-rich foods such as whole grains, vegetables and fruit is more beneficial than probiotic supplements for maintaining gut microbiome diversity. A farm worker harvests barley in Brandenburg state, Germany. [Getty Images] If you have been faithfully taking probiotics but are not noticing any real difference in your digestive health, it may be worth ditching the supplements and simply changing your diet instead. The Washington Post reported Thursday that there is little evidence probiotic supplements improve gut health in healthy people. Citing research by Kira L. Newman, a clinical assistant professor at the University of Michigan Medical School published in the journal Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology, the Post said that "for most people, probiotics may provide a sense of agency, but may not necessarily deliver the benefits users are looking for." Some research has even found that in certain cases, probiotic supplements can disrupt the composition of the gut microbiome — the complex community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract. The research found that while probiotic supplements contain microorganisms capable of activating the gut, their numbers are limited and they often fail to function effectively. Some studies have found that probiotic supplements actually reduce microbiome diversity. A Stanford University research team conducted a clinical trial in which adults with metabolic syndrome took probiotic supplements for 18 weeks. Some participants showed improvements in blood pressure and triglyceride levels, but others saw their blood sugar and insulin levels worsen. One reason probiotics often fall short of expectations is that they struggle to reach the intestines intact after passing through the digestive tract. The research team pointed to fiber-rich foods — fruits, vegetables and whole grains — as a more promising alternative. Newman said foods such as fruits, vegetables and whole grains all support a healthy microbiome, adding that dietary fiber acts as fuel for the gut's microbial community. "Most of our guidelines for gastrointestinal health and microbiome-related conditions do not recommend probiotics on a routine basis," Newman said. "What we consistently recommend across many conditions is a diet rich in fruits, vegetables and whole grains." Fiber stands apart from probiotics not only because it feeds the microbiome, but also because it arrives in the intestines undamaged. The human body lacks the enzymes needed to break down fiber, so it passes through intact. Gut microorganisms then convert fiber into short-chain fatty acids and other compounds that help reduce inflammation, improve blood sugar levels and stimulate the production of appetite-suppressing hormones. Newman also said that fermented foods — such as yogurt, kimchi and kefir — can alter the composition of the gut microbiome and promote gut health. Research suggests that eating fiber-rich plants alongside fermented foods can increase microbiome diversity and help crowd out harmful pathogens. kate01@heraldcorp.com This content was produced with the assistance of AI translation services.

cb2d5081-787c-4ad0-af81-c0cabee7aa0c.title: Herself battling cancer, city woman helps fellow warriors with protein powder
cb2d5081-787c-4ad0-af81-c0cabee7aa0c.incipit: When Sangita Patnaik (55) was diagnosed with stage-II breast cancer in Dec 2024, her life went for a toss. A businesswoman, running a...
cb2d5081-787c-4ad0-af81-c0cabee7aa0c.body: When Sangita Patnaik (55) was diagnosed with stage-II breast cancer in Dec 2024, her life went for a toss. A businesswoman, running a beauty parlour and lassi counter in the city, Sangita could no longer work for long stretches. The disease took away her appetite, sleep and even the strength to get through a normal day. But one thing it couldn’t take away was her zest for life and desire to help others. Somewhere between chemo, radiation and hormone therapy, she found a reason to look beyond her own pain. For a woman who loves to work, she couldn’t just sit idle during her treatment while also listening to the nutritional needs of her body. That is when she came up with the idea of making a protein powder, not just for herself but also for her fellow warriors who couldn’t afford costly protein supplements. For the past year, the Bhubaneswar woman has been making protein powder and other nutritious food items in her kitchen and giving them for free to poor cancer patients and survivors. “I felt everything inside me was burning. There were many sleepless nights, and there still are. But if I had just sat down, I would have gone into depression. So, I decided to channel whatever strength I had towards helping poor cancer patients,” Sangita said. A mother who has always loved cooking, she started experimenting in her kitchen with dry fruits, grains and pulses to prepare a protein-rich powder. What began as something she made for herself soon became an effort to help others. “During cancer treatment and recovery, the body needs protein to repair tissues, maintain muscle and support recovery. I learnt this from my doctors. But protein supplements are not affordable for everyone,” she said, adding she realised the importance of nutrition during treatment. “I know how difficult it can be for a poor patient undergoing chemotherapy,” she said. Sangita buys the ingredients herself, prepares the powder at home under hygienic conditions and packs it for distribution. Her son and his friends help distribute the packets at hospitals, old-age homes, orphanages and slum settlements. Someone who has always believed in ‘seva’, Sangita has been helping elderly people in unregistered old-age homes, providing residents with rations, clothes and other necessities. Sangita also runs a small kitchen where she makes pickles, papads, badi and other food products. A large part of the earnings goes towards the initiative. Her son and daughter, both engineers, also contribute to the effort, as do people who have learnt about her work through social media. For Sangita, the packets leaving her kitchen are more than food. They have become a way of making sense of the difficult year she has lived through. She said it is her way of fighting back not only against the cancer body but also the helplessness that often accompanies the disease. “I may not be able to do much, but whatever strength I have, I want to use it for someone who needs it,” she said.

3f24fd42-01b4-4812-9875-945e27e4bfac.title: When’s the Best Time to Take Magnesium?
3f24fd42-01b4-4812-9875-945e27e4bfac.incipit: The internet is buzzing about magnesium supplements: the benefits of taking magnesium, the different types of magnesium that are available, and how to time your supplementation to max out the benefits. But...
3f24fd42-01b4-4812-9875-945e27e4bfac.body: The internet is buzzing about magnesium supplements : the benefits of taking magnesium , the different types of magnesium that are available, and how to time your supplementation to max out the benefits. But before we get into the latter, it’s important to recognize that while there is a time for magnesium, there is also a place. And that place is not always in your supplement routine. “Influencers and health coaches have exaggerated the need for supplementation,” says Maddie Pasquariello, MS, RD . “Most people can get enough magnesium through food without making drastic or expensive changes to their diet, and we should be encouraging this before telling everyone to supplement.” Indeed, there are many common magnesium-rich foods that can easily cover the 400–420 milligrams that the National Institutes of Health recommend for men over 19 years old. Of course, if for whatever reason you aren’t able to get enough magnesium through your regular diet, supplements can help. And, in that case, you’ll want to make sure you’re aware of the best times to take magnesium, whether you should be taking it with or without food, and any other considerations that might help you get more bang for your buck. So here’s everything you need to know. Your body doesn’t care what time you take your magnesium According to Pasquariello, it’s much more important that you’re getting enough magnesium than exactly what time of day you’re taking it. “We just don’t have an abundance of evidence to suggest that timing your magnesium to a specific moment in your day makes a huge difference for most people,” she says. That said, it makes sense that a more readily absorbed form of magnesium would take effect more quickly—something worth considering if you’re taking magnesium specifically to address your sleep . “For easily absorbed forms of magnesium that exert a bit of a relaxing effect, like magnesium glycinate, taking it before you go to sleep might be most effective,” Pasquariello says. Similarly, the specific type of magnesium you’re taking might come with side effects that could influence when you take it. “Many people prefer to take magnesium with their morning meal, especially because some forms—especially those that are mild laxatives—can cause a bit of immediate digestive change that you don’t want right before you go to bed,” Pasquariello says. “On the other hand, some people find that the effects on reducing constipation are best felt after a night of sleep. So it might just require a bit of trial and error to figure out what works best for you.” If you are low on magnesium, consistency is more important than timing Diagnosing a magnesium deficiency can be tricky, as much of your body’s magnesium is not found in the blood . While urine tests and other diagnostic pathways can help you and your doctor get a handle on your magnesium levels, Pasquariello recommends that those concerned about their magnesium intake start with a simple dietary audit. “If you’re not getting enough magnesium as evidenced by an audit of your diet or testing, your practitioner would probably recommend a daily supplement, but it’s important to only supplement if you know that you need to,” she says. If you do, in fact, need to supplement with magnesium, consistency should be your main priority. Whereas a handful of specific supplements, like high-dose vitamin D or iron, can be taken once or twice a week, magnesium supplements should be taken daily. “Like most supplements, it’s not one-and-done with magnesium,” Pasquariello says. “If you’re not getting enough through your diet and can’t manage to do so by making dietary tweaks, taking a magnesium supplement just once a week or whenever you remember to is likely not going to be enough.” Ultimately, when it comes to raising your overall magnesium levels and optimizing the myriad bodily processes that magnesium is involved in, don’t worry about timing right away and focus instead on what will allow you to be most consistent. “This is best achieved by taking it at the same time every day,” Pasquariello says. “From there, you can test out various timings and see how your body responds.” Timing your magnesium supplements could help you manage their side effects If you find that, regardless of time of day, your magnesium supplement consistently triggers unwanted side effects, like an upset stomach or diarrhea, splitting your dose into two or more servings may help mitigate the unwanted effects. “It will depend slightly on the total dose you are taking, but for some people, larger doses may be more easily tolerated when spread out throughout the day,” Pasquariello says. “For most people, though, taking it daily in one go is just as effective as taking it both morning and night, so for convenience and efficiency—and ensuring you actually remember to take it—one shot is what I’d recommend here.” Alternatively, you may find that your magnesium supplement is better tolerated when taken together with a meal. Technically speaking, as a mineral, magnesium itself is neither fat-soluble nor water-soluble, meaning its absorption won’t be influenced by the foods you consume it with. Regardless, “some people report fewer negative side effects when taking magnesium with food, most likely due to the laxative effects that certain forms can have,” Pasquariello says. “So if you cannot get enough magnesium through your diet and it’s recommended that you supplement, I would start by taking it with food and seeing how you feel.”

ed6b372b-cc9b-4467-99f3-07a7243d1c07.title: Oklahoma State Fair expands accessibility with sensory-friendly hours
ed6b372b-cc9b-4467-99f3-07a7243d1c07.incipit: The Oklahoma State Fair is increasing efforts to be more inclusive for attendees with disabilities.A designated "Sensory-Friendly Time" will offer a less stimulating...
ed6b372b-cc9b-4467-99f3-07a7243d1c07.body: SThe Oklahoma State Fair is increasing efforts to be more inclusive for attendees with disabilities. A designated "Sensory-Friendly Time" will offer a less stimulating experience for fairgoers. New accessibility features include calming stations, an expo, and a gluten-free food stand. When most people think of a state fair, they think of sensory overload: The dazzling, dizzying look and feel of riding carnival rides, the sound and reverberation of music played live and loud, the scents and tastes of deep-fried delicacies and other exotic, elaborate foods. But people who visit the Oklahoma State Fair in the morning and early afternoon on Sunday, Sept. 20, will find a more muted, less glaring experience. That's because 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sept. 20 has been designated Sensory-Friendly Time , with special activities for attendees who need a quieter and less brightly lit fair experience. The Sensory-Friendly Time, which was previously offered during the final weekend of the fair, is a way of making one of the state's largest annual events accessible to people who are on the autism spectrum or have sensory processing challenges. "We're trying to be all-inclusive. We also have the calming rooms around the property for people that have got sensory overload and need to decompress a little bit," said longtime state fair spokesman Scott Munz . "We're constantly trying to upgrade ... because we want everybody to enjoy the fair." Featuring about 100 events and activities — many of them free with outside gate admission — every day, the Oklahoma State Fair continues through Sunday, Sept. 27, at OKC Fair Park, 3001 General Pershing Blvd. About 800,000 to 1 million people attend the Oklahoma State Fair annually, Munz said, and one way organizers are trying to bring in more visitors is by boosting efforts to help people with disabilities, allergies and other challenges experience the event. "We want to be as inclusive as possible," he said. "You're never going to hit everything. But we're going to try." Along with Sensory-Friendly Time, the 2026 Oklahoma State Fair includes events like the second annual Accessibility Expo and the fifth annual Equine Empowerment Horse Show as well as attractions like the Momentum Refresh mobile restroom and universal changing station, all designed to make the event more accessible . "Accessibility is at the heart of building an inclusive community, and our continued partnership with the Oklahoma State Fair shows that everyone is welcome to join in the tradition and fun that the fair has to offer,” said Jenifer Randle, executive director of the Developmental Disabilities Council of Oklahoma , in an email. Accessibility programs the Oklahoma State Fair is offering this year include: Sensory-Friendly Time When and where: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 20, throughout OKC Fair Park. For those who find the sights, sounds and crowds of the Oklahoma State Fair overstimulating, the morning and early afternoon of the first Sunday of the event have been designated Sensory-Friendly Time , with special activities for attendees who need a less noisy and bright fair experience. Accessibility Expo When and where: Noon to 5 p.m. Sunday, Sept. 20, Modern Living Building. Added to the state fair in 2025 , the Accessibility Expo is designed as a celebration of inclusion, innovation and community that includes organizations, artists, vendors and advocates working to support and empower disabled Oklahomans and their families. The event features exhibitor booths, interactive art activities and performances by community organizations providing arts access to disabled Oklahomans. Equine Empowerment Horse Show When and where: 9 a.m. Tuesday, Sept. 22, Performance Arena. The fifth annual Equine Empowerment Horse Show is for equestrians with disabilities, and several classes have been added for veterans. The event is intended to provide an opportunity for these horse lovers to compete and engage in an activity rarely afforded them, while showing off their determination, skill and talent in the arena. Momentum Refresh When and where: 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily, The Circle, in front of the Modern Living Building. For the third consecutive year the state fair is hosting Momentum Refresh, a first-of-its-kind mobile restroom and universal changing station. It is a private, fully accessible space equipped with specialized amenities, including a large changing table with a ceiling hoist, room for caregivers and a dedicated calming and lactation room. Sponsored by the Developmental Disabilities Council, the space is staffed by trained personnel who assist visitors with using the vehicle and clean it between uses. “We’re excited to return to the Oklahoma State Fair to ensure everyone has the opportunity to participate and enjoy the spirit of community," said Dan Lusk, executive director of Momentum Refresh, in a statement. “ Momentum Refresh is designed so no one has to cut their day short or worry about how they’ll handle a personal care break at the fair." Adult changing stations When and where: Daily, four locations. In addition to the Momentum Refresh mobile restroom, OKC Fair Park is equipped with four permanent adult changing stations that are accessible during the Oklahoma State Fair: in the OG&E Coliseum for patrons of ticketed events like "Disney on Ice;" in the main lobby of the Bennett Event Center; and in each of the men’s and women’s restrooms at the Bandshell Stage. Calming stations When and where: Daily, three locations. During the fair, designated calming stations are available in the Momentum Refresh trailer, in the Arts Annex and near Gate 9. These spaces are available for fairgoers who need a break from the hustle and bustle, including people on the autism spectrum or those who have sensory processing challenges. Square Holes , a local neurodiversity consulting firm, and the Developmental Disabilities Council of Oklahoma, assisted in the development of these areas. Everybody Eats When and where: Open daily, on Gordon Cooper Boulevard, across from the Pavilion. A new food stand for the 2026 Oklahoma State Fair, Everybody Eats is serving up gluten-free corn dogs, deep-fried Oreos, chicken strips and funnel cakes. The stand sells only gluten-free items made with gluten-free ingredients using dedicated fryers by employees who have received allergen training; ingredient lists are available upon request. 87921e3b-a301-49e6-bea9-6fcc40fa2420.title: Canadian ambassador visits Seattle, seeks to strengthen ties with Washington state
87921e3b-a301-49e6-bea9-6fcc40fa2420.incipit: A U.S. ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian products went into effect at midnight, marking the latest escalation in a trade war...
87921e3b-a301-49e6-bea9-6fcc40fa2420.body: SEATTLE — A U.S. ban on nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian products went into effect at midnight, marking the latest escalation in a trade war between the United States and Canada. The ban applies to a range of products, including alcohol, certain dairy products and motorcycles. Experts say consumers may not notice an immediate impact because of existing inventory and some exemptions. The president said he expects Canada to return to the negotiating table soon. The restriction comes as the Canadian ambassador to the United States visited Seattle to celebrate trade relations between Washington state and Canada. RELATED | US bans Canadian booze, dairy and motorcycles as trade war escalates Seattle resident Mike Sandberg said he has long viewed the relationship between the neighboring countries as close. “I’ve always thought of it as brothers or cousins,” Sandberg said. “We should just be getting along,” he added, later saying, “They seem like they don’t like us very much right now.” Strained relations have grown more tense as the Trump administration moves to block nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian imports, including certain dairy products, alcoholic drinks and motorcycles. The ban is described as the latest counterpunch by the U.S., striking back after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of American goods following the White House’s imposition of 50% tariffs last month. Canadian Ambassador to the U.S. Mark Wiseman said the tariffs are already being felt in Canada. The tariffs are having a big impact,” Wiseman said. “The 232 tariffs and now, more recently, the 338 [tariffs] are having a big impact on certain sectors of the Canadian economy, whether that’s those involved in steel and aluminum or auto manufacturing or forest products. We believe that those tariffs should not be in place. As consumers in both countries deal with the effects, Sandberg said, “They shouldn’t be tariffing us, and we shouldn’t be tariffing them.” Wiseman said efforts are underway to strengthen ties with Washington state, citing Canadian investment and jobs. “We’re doing a lot of business in Washington State,” he said. “Canadian companies employ over 30,000 workers here in Washington.” Sandberg said he does not believe the countries should be at odds. “It seems like we shouldn’t be in an adversarial relationship with Canada. I mean, they’re our buddies,” he said. He also said, “It hurts our business when they don’t come.” Wiseman said he hopes the dispute eases. “Hopefully, we’ll get to a place where all restrictions on both sides of the border come down,” he said. Canada is not expected to retaliate further, according to the Canadian prime minister.

ade4cf96-3efb-4293-803d-44a1a63a7262.title: Popular Joint Supplement Linked to 25% Higher Dementia Risk in People With Early Memory Loss
ade4cf96-3efb-4293-803d-44a1a63a7262.incipit: Over the past two decades, the sale of dietary supplements has taken off.Today, it seems as though there's a pill for practically any ailment you can think of.While the benefits might seem hopeful, there's...
ade4cf96-3efb-4293-803d-44a1a63a7262.body: Over the past two decades, the sale of dietary supplements has taken off. Today, it seems as though there's a pill for practically any ailment you can think of. While the benefits might seem hopeful, there's reason to tread cautiously. Some supplements can be costly and offer little to no benefits . Others may have unexpected downsides . A new study underlines the potential for harm. The preliminary analysis, published in Nature Metabolism , finds initial evidence that a popular supplement, taken by more than 40 million Americans , is associated with faster progression to dementia in people with early memory problems. Glucosamine is a natural sugar-related molecule widely sold over the counter as a supplement in the US. It is especially popular among older adults, who use it to support joint health and manage arthritis symptoms or joint discomfort. But it may have an insidious downside for a certain subset of older adults. Using electronic health record data, researchers at the University of Florida (UF) have now found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25 percent higher likelihood that mild cognitive impairment would progress to dementia. "People take the supplement based on anecdotal reports that it improves joint health, especially in the knees," writes biochemist Ramon Sun from UF for The Conversation. Glucosamine is widely sold over the counter as a supplement in the US. (Sveta615/Canva) Glucosamine is known to cross the blood-brain barrier, but what it might do to influence dementia progression is unknown. "A lesser-known problem associated with Alzheimer's disease is that brain cells and proteins build up extra sugar coatings," explains Sun. Glucosamine allows the body to make sugar chains, called glycans, that can be attached to proteins. Analyzing the postmortem brain tissue of three people who died with Alzheimer's disease, researchers at UF measured a global increase in glycan structures compared to three healthy controls. In another set of brain samples grouped by disease stage, the more advanced the Alzheimer's, the more of these sugary structures researchers observed in the gray matter of patients. In fact, these 'sugar decorations' could be a possible hallmark of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. "Proteins are the cell's molecular machines, and many of them need sugar tags added in just the right way to fold correctly, travel to the right place, and do their jobs," explains molecular biologist Matt Gentry from UF. "What we found in Alzheimer's is that this sugar-tagging system appears to be overactive. The Alzheimer's brain is adding too many of these sugar structures, and this seems to contribute to the disease rather than protect against it." Earlier research has linked glucosamine supplements to a lower dementia risk in cognitively healthy adults. But what if the brain's metabolism is disrupted? Could glucosamine be feeding into the issue? An emerging hypothesis suggests that Alzheimer's disease is actually a metabolic disorder at its core. Some researchers have even gone so far as to call it "type 3 diabetes ". "The adverse effects of glucosamine may be contingent on an underlying neurometabolic state," researchers at UF hypothesize . To find out if that is true, Sun and colleagues analyzed the health records of 24,000 patients with dementia and 41,000 with mild cognitive impairment. Roughly 8 percent of this combined cohort was taking glucosamine. Among those who already had Alzheimer's disease or related dementias, glucosamine use was associated with a 25 percent higher mortality risk within five years. This does not mean that glucosamine is necessarily causing the progression of Alzheimer's. That would require a randomized controlled trial to confirm. But given the popularity of these supplements and their potential harm, further investigation is needed. "The electronic health record data are very provocative," says Gentry. "While it's an association and not proof of causality, it does raise an important clinical question that now deserves much more attention." The results are bolstered by a mouse experiment. Gentry and colleagues conducted a follow-up in animals that were genetically engineered to have Alzheimer's-like symptoms. When the team blocked the enzyme that makes sugars like glucosamine, dementia symptoms in the mice improved. What's more, when researchers fed the mice glucosamine, their memory loss worsened. Interestingly, however, healthy mice given the same supplement showed no effect. The findings suggest that glucosamine may be driving cognitive decline, but only in some cases. To see if the results hold up in humans, Sun says he and his colleagues hope to follow dementia patients who once took glucosamine and then discontinued it. Their goal is to investigate how their disease fares compared to those who remain on the supplement. In an accompanying piece for Nature , biochemist Yasuhiko Kizuka, who was not involved in the study, writes that these 'sugar decorations' in the Alzheimer's brain may be a novel drug target. "This study reveals that hyperglycosylation of proteins is a new hallmark of Alzheimer's," Kizuka writes . "The work not only enhances our understanding of the pathological mechanism of Alzheimer's but also provides a new strategy for combating this devastating disease." If nothing else, the findings are a good reminder to stay skeptical when adding a supplement to your daily routine. The benefits might look good in one meta-analysis , but not everyone will necessarily have the same response. There might even be risks. The research has been published in Nature Metabolism . This article was fact-checked by Rebecca Dyer and edited by Rebecca Dyer . While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know .

1e1430b0-53b9-4527-870a-2b5c1b14bee8.title: She is almost 101 years old: the centenarian shared what she starts each morning with and what she considers most important in life
1e1430b0-53b9-4527-870a-2b5c1b14bee8.incipit: As TODAY reports, Greger was born in 1925 in Brooklyn. She got married at 21, worked as a telephone operator, lived with her husband for 68 years, raised two children, and today has four grandchildren and six great-grandchildren. Now, Natalie lives
1e1430b0-53b9-4527-870a-2b5c1b14bee8.body: As TODAY reports, Greger was born in 1925 in Brooklyn. She got married at 21, worked as a telephone operator, lived with her husband for 68 years, raised two children, and today has four grandchildren and six great-grandchildren. Now, Natalie lives in a care facility in Englewood, New Jersey. When asked about the secret to longevity, she simply replies: one must remain open to the world, accept life as it is, and enjoy it. ### Starting the day with blueberries Natalie's breakfast invariably begins with blueberries — she admits that she loves these berries very much. Her diet also includes a lot of apples and avocados. At the same time, the centenarian does not follow any special diet: according to her, she eats almost everything. TODAY notes that blueberries are associated with benefits for the cardiovascular system, a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes, and the maintenance of cognitive functions. Apples and avocados are also among the foods that researchers associate with various health benefits. ### Not denying yourself favorite foods Natalie loves chocolate, especially dark chocolate. But there is also a food in her menu that dietitians would hardly recommend eating often — bacon. For breakfast, she might have two fried eggs with bacon and an English muffin. The centenarian herself jokes that she probably shouldn't eat bacon, but she does anyway. However, the authors of the article specifically warn: the diet of a particular centenarian should not be taken as a universal recipe. Experts note that people who live to such an advanced age may possess a rare combination of protective genetic factors. Natalie does not consume alcohol. Even at her 101st birthday celebration, she plans to raise a glass not with alcohol, but with a soft drink. On the table, there will also be another of her favorite dishes — mushroom pizza. ### Dancing while there’s a chance Dancing has accompanied Natalie for almost her entire life. She loved ballroom dancing and taught her husband to dance. On Sundays after breakfast, the couple would play records and dance around the living room and dining room. At 20, Natalie danced at the Brooklyn Academy of Music and recalls that she could lift her legs almost like the famous Rockettes troupe members. At 100, her capabilities are different, but she hasn’t given up music — she now dances while sitting in a chair. Dancing combines physical activity with coordination and balance training, and moreover, it provides an opportunity to socialize and experience positive emotions. ### Finding an activity that calms As a girl, Natalie learned to knit from her mother. For many years, she knitted blankets, hats, and sweaters and only gave up her favorite hobby a couple of years ago due to hand problems. TODAY cites studies linking crafting with improved emotional well-being: such activities can help relax and cope with stress. Now, Natalie also plays solitaire on her iPad and plays the card game canasta with friends. The article notes that board and card games are associated with maintaining cognitive functions in old age. ### Not taking troubles too close to heart Natalie considers herself a happy person. She loves to laugh, joke, and tries not to dwell on life’s problems. According to her, she does not belong to people who constantly discuss their troubles, and she believes that this approach makes her life easier. The authors of the article remind that chronic stress is linked to adverse health outcomes, while psychological resilience and the ability to regulate emotions can help cope with its effects. ### Believing that everything will be fine Another trait of Natalie is optimism. Even after going through tough times, she continues to believe that in the end, everything will be fine. Studies cited by TODAY have found a link between higher levels of optimism and greater longevity. However, this refers to a statistical correlation, not a guaranteed way to live to a hundred. Natalie Greger's story shows that her personal formula for longevity is surprisingly simple: eat a varied diet without strict prohibitions, stay active, maintain favorite hobbies, socialize with people, and try not to let life's difficulties take away joy. And every morning, she still starts with her favorite blueberries.

704a427c-21a8-46cb-87ff-39615a175059.body: COLUMBIA, Mo. (KMIZ) Protein is everywhere. Grocery stores are full of products that promise extra protein, and federal health authorities have sung the virtues of adding more to Americans' diets. But a University of Missouri Health Care doctor said Tuesday that there's not much evidence to show that "protein maxxing" has any health benefits. The American Medical Association defines "protein maxxing" as a trend "where users focus on maximizing dietary protein intake to boost metabolism, manage weight and build muscle". University of Missouri School of Medicine Senior Associate Dean of Research Bettina Mittendorfer said there is little evidence that adding excessive protein to your diet improves muscle strength. "If you protein max because you think you're going to build more muscle, you become stronger, there's no evidence really that this works," Mittendorfer said. Mittendorfer added that excessive protein intake can raise health concerns. "High protein intake, particularly high protein intake from animal sources, meats, dairy products, and things like that, is associated with greater risks of developing Type 2 diabetes. They're also associated with a greater risk of developing heart disease," Mittendorfer said. The standard recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.36 grams per pound of body weight for a healthy adult. When asked why Mittendorfer thinks this "protein-maxxing" trend has become popular, she said that it comes down to the other food groups falling out of favor and protein being easy to sell. "So I think this is sort of if I'm not supposed to eat carbs, if I'm not supposed to eat fat, I gotta eat something to eat the protein," Mittendorfer said. Catherine Peterson, an associate director and associate professor of nutrition and exercise physiology at the University of Missouri, said that she was unfamiliar with the trend, but she does know about the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services coming out with recommendations called the Dietary Guidelines for Americans that are roughly double the recommended daily allowance. Peterson said that there are four tenets of good nutrition, and if you violate one or more, you could be facing risks. "You're kind of playing a little bit with some possible risks that we don't even know, either foreseen or unforeseen, because you are throwing off balance," Peterson said when talking about violating one of the tenets. Peterson stressed eating plant-based protein to provide other nutrients, like fiber. "Because at least you get in some of the other goodies that plants provide, like fiber and phytochemicals and vitamins and minerals," Peterson said. Peterson said too much protein compromises gut health. She recommends keeping a balanced diet with fruit, vegetables, and grain alongside protein. Peterson recommends not exceeding 0.9 grams of protein per pound of body weight.
